steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the history and status section of an encyclopedia article on array database management systems (Array DBMSs): why the relational model falls short for arrays, the key research and implementations so far, and where the technology stands now.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Relational model and SQL don't support arrays well; BLOBs
- Early work beyond BLOBs
- Query languages and theory
- Implementations
- Sparse vs dense data
- Current status and open questions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Relational model
  - prevailing; doesn't directly support arrays like sets and tuples
  - ISO SQL array-valued attribute: one-dimensional, almost no operational support, not usable for Array DBMS domains
  - BLOBs ("binary large objects"): like files, byte strings of (conceptually) unlimited length; no query functionality e.g. multi-dimensional subsetting
- Beyond BLOBs
  - PICDMS first significant work (cite); precursor of 2-D array query language; procedural, no suitable storage support
- Languages / theory
  - Baumann: first declarative query language for multiple dimensions, algebra-based semantics, scalable architecture (cite x2)
  - Marathe and Salem: array database language, 2-D only (cite)
  - Libkin et al.: seminal theory, NCRA, nested relational calculus + multidimensional arrays, array query complexity analysis (cite)
  - Mennis et al.: map algebra for 2-D and 3-D spatial raster data (cite)
- Implementations
  - rasdaman: longest track record, n-D arrays, full query support
  - Oracle GeoRaster: chunked 2-D raster maps, no SQL integration
  - TerraLib: open-source GIS, extends object-relational DBMS for spatio-temporal types; mainly vector, some raster
  - PostGIS 2.0: 2-D raster support; special function for declarative raster queries
  - SciQL: array query language being added to MonetDB
  - SciDB: more recent; arrays as tables (like SciQL) vs new attribute type (rasdaman, PostGIS)
- Sparse vs dense
  - OLAP data cubes established for sparse data; store values with location, compression when few valid locations; SQL
  - doesn't scale in density; dense data (satellite images) -> proprietary ad hoc implementations in scientific data management
  - so Array DBMSs can contribute here
- Status
  - emerging technology; deployed: Oracle GeoRaster, PostGIS 2.0, rasdaman
  - open questions: query language design and formalization, optimization, parallelization/distribution, scalability
  - scientific communities reluctant, favor specialized proprietary tech

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Today the prevailing data model is the relational one, and it does not directly support the array paradigm the way it supports sets and tuples. ISO SQL does list an array-valued attribute type, but it is only one-dimensional, there is almost no operational support for it, and it can't be used for the application domains of Array DBMSs. Another option is to use BLOBs ("binary large objects"), which are equivalent to files: byte strings of (conceptually) unlimited length. But again there is no query language functionality, for example multi-dimensional subsetting.

The first significant work going beyond BLOBs was PICDMS. This system offers the precursor of a 2-D array query language, but it is still procedural and doesn't have suitable storage support.

Baumann published a first declarative query language that is suitable for multiple dimensions and has an algebra-based semantics, together with a scalable architecture. Marathe and Salem presented another array database language, but it is constrained to 2-D. Libkin et al. did seminal theoretical work. Their model is called NCRA and it extends a nested relational calculus with multidimensional arrays, and among the results there are important contributions on the complexity analysis of array queries. Mennis et al. published a map algebra which is suitable for 2-D and 3-D spatial raster data.

- implementations
  - rasdaman: longest track record, n-D, full query support
  - Oracle GeoRaster: chunked 2-D raster maps, no SQL integration
  - TerraLib: open-source GIS on object-relational DBMS, spatio-temporal; mainly vector, some raster
  - PostGIS 2.0: 2-D rasters, special function for declarative raster queries
  - SciQL being added to MonetDB; SciDB more recent; both treat arrays as tables, unlike rasdaman/PostGIS (new attribute type)
- sparse vs dense
  - OLAP data cubes for sparse data (values + location, compression, SQL)
  - doesn't scale in density -> dense data like satellite images handled by proprietary ad hoc implementations
  - opening for Array DBMSs
- status
  - emerging; deployed: Oracle GeoRaster, PostGIS 2.0, rasdaman
  - open: query language design/formalization, optimization, parallelization/distribution, scalability
  - scientific communities reluctant, prefer proprietary tech

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Today the prevailing data model is the relational one, and it does not directly support the array paradigm the way it supports sets and tuples. ISO SQL does list an array-valued attribute type, but it is only one-dimensional, there is almost no operational support for it, and it can't be used for the application domains of Array DBMSs. Another option is to use BLOBs ("binary large objects"), which are equivalent to files: byte strings of (conceptually) unlimited length. But again there is no query language functionality, for example multi-dimensional subsetting.

The first significant work going beyond BLOBs was PICDMS. This system offers the precursor of a 2-D array query language, but it is still procedural and doesn't have suitable storage support.

Baumann published a first declarative query language that is suitable for multiple dimensions and has an algebra-based semantics, together with a scalable architecture. Marathe and Salem presented another array database language, but it is constrained to 2-D. Libkin et al. did seminal theoretical work. Their model is called NCRA and it extends a nested relational calculus with multidimensional arrays, and among the results there are important contributions on the complexity analysis of array queries. Mennis et al. published a map algebra which is suitable for 2-D and 3-D spatial raster data.

As for implementations of Array DBMSs, the rasdaman system has the longest track record of implementing n-D arrays with full query support. Oracle GeoRaster has chunked storage of 2-D raster maps, but no SQL integration. TerraLib is open-source GIS software which extends object-relational DBMS technology so it can handle spatio-temporal data types; its main focus is vector data, but there is also some support for rasters. PostGIS embeds raster support for 2-D rasters starting with version 2.0, and a special function offers declarative raster query functionality. SciQL is an array query language that is being added to the MonetDB DBMS. SciDB is a more recent initiative to establish array database support. In SciDB, like in SciQL, arrays are seen as equivalent to tables, and not as a new attribute type like in rasdaman and PostGIS.

OLAP data cubes are well established for the special case of sparse data. They store cell values together with their location, which is an adequate compression technique when only a few locations carry valid information at all, and they operate on them with SQL. This technique does not scale in density, so standard databases are not used today for dense data like satellite images, where most cells carry meaningful information. Instead proprietary ad hoc implementations prevail in scientific data management and similar situations. So this is where Array DBMSs can make a particular contribution.

In general Array DBMSs are an emerging technology. There are operationally deployed systems, like Oracle GeoRaster, PostGIS 2.0 and rasdaman, but there are still many open research questions, including query language design and formalization, query optimization, parallelization and distributed processing, and scalability issues in general. Also, scientific communities still seem reluctant to take up array database technology and tend to prefer specialized, proprietary technology.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The relational data model, which prevails today, does not directly support the array paradigm to the same extent as sets and tuples. ISO SQL lists an array-valued attribute type, but it is only one-dimensional, has almost no operational support, and is not usable for the application domains of Array DBMSs. Another option is to resort to BLOBs ("binary large objects"), which are equivalent to files: byte strings of (conceptually) unlimited length, but again without any query language functionality such as multi-dimensional subsetting.

The first significant work going beyond BLOBs was PICDMS.[1] This system offers the precursor of a 2-D array query language, although it is still procedural and lacks suitable storage support.

A first declarative query language suitable for multiple dimensions and with algebra-based semantics was published by Baumann, together with a scalable architecture.[2,3] Another array database language, constrained to 2-D, was presented by Marathe and Salem.[4] Seminal theoretical work was done by Libkin et al.;[5] in their model, called NCRA, they extend a nested relational calculus with multidimensional arrays, and their results include important contributions on array query complexity analysis. A map algebra suitable for 2-D and 3-D spatial raster data has been published by Mennis et al.[6]

In terms of Array DBMS implementations, the rasdaman system has the longest implementation track record of n-D arrays with full query support. Oracle GeoRaster offers chunked storage of 2-D raster maps, although without SQL integration. TerraLib is open-source GIS software that extends object-relational DBMS technology to handle spatio-temporal data types; while its main focus is on vector data, there is also some support for rasters. Starting with version 2.0, PostGIS embeds support for 2-D rasters, and a special function offers declarative raster query functionality. SciQL is an array query language being added to the MonetDB DBMS. SciDB is a more recent initiative to establish array database support. As in SciQL, arrays are seen as equivalent to tables rather than as a new attribute type as in rasdaman and PostGIS.

For the special case of sparse data, OLAP data cubes are well established; they store cell values together with their location, an adequate compression technique given the few locations carrying valid information at all, and operate on them with SQL. Since this technique does not scale in density, standard databases are not used today for dense data such as satellite images, where most cells carry meaningful information; instead, proprietary ad hoc implementations prevail in scientific data management and similar situations. This is therefore where Array DBMSs can make a particular contribution.

Generally, Array DBMSs are an emerging technology. While operationally deployed systems exist, such as Oracle GeoRaster, PostGIS 2.0 and rasdaman, many open research questions remain, including query language design and formalization, query optimization, parallelization and distributed processing, and scalability issues in general. Besides, scientific communities still seem reluctant to take up array database technology and tend to favor specialized, proprietary technology.
